Neonatal sandbar sharks emerge from their mothers at a total length of approximately 64 cm [Lb = approximately 64 cm], a size that reflects the extensive provisioning received during a lengthy gestation period. Following a gestation that lasts about 409 days [ab = about 409 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the pups are born in shallow, coastal nursery grounds where they benefit from warm, productive waters that support rapid early growth. The thermal regime of these nursery habitats, typically around 27 °C [T = 27 °C], appears critical for efficient yolk utilization and the onset of independent foraging. During this early life stage, the young sharks are particularly vulnerable to predation, but their relatively large birth size confers a degree of protection compared to smaller elasmobranch neonates. This substantial initial length is a common feature among carcharhinid sharks and is thought to be linked to the species' K-selected life-history strategy, which prioritizes offspring quality over quantity.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is pronounced in the sandbar shark, with females attaining a considerably larger ultimate total length than males. Mature females can reach a maximum total length of 250 cm [Li = 250 cm], whereas males achieve a more modest terminal size of 180 cm [Li = 180 cm]. This size disparity is reflected in the species' reproductive ecology, as larger females are capable of carrying and nourishing more developing embryos during their 12-month gestation cycles. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown female is correspondingly substantial, with the heaviest individuals recorded at approximately 117,900 grams [Wwi = approximately 117,900 grams]. This large body mass is supported by a diet dominated by benthic fishes and invertebrates, and it enables females to store sufficient energy reserves to fuel the energetic demands of reproduction, including the production of relatively large litters.

Puberty in the sandbar shark is reached at different sizes depending on sex, and these milestones are typically assessed by measuring fork length. Females attain sexual maturity when their fork length reaches approximately 154.9 cm [Lp = approximately 154.9 cm], a size that is usually achieved after a period of steady somatic growth. Males, in contrast, begin the pubertal transition at a slightly smaller fork length of about 151.6 cm [Lp = about 151.6 cm]. Under a stable thermal environment of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the time since birth at which these pubertal lengths are attained is estimated at roughly 13 years [tp = roughly 13 years], a prolonged juvenile phase that underscores the species' slow pace of life. This delayed maturation is characteristic of many large, long-lived elasmobranchs and is a key factor in their vulnerability to overfishing.

Reproductive output in the sandbar shark is characterized by modest litter sizes and a biennial or triennial breeding cycle for most females. Litter sizes typically range from just 1 to 8 pups per year [Ri = 1 to 8 pups per year], a relatively low fecundity compared to many teleost fishes. This annual reproductive output represents the maximum observed rate under favorable environmental conditions, one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], and it yields a daily reproductive rate that is inherently low. The stable temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] that characterizes their core habitat is thought to be optimal for sustaining the metabolic costs of gestation and for ensuring adequate yolk provisioning to the developing pups. Such a low annual fecundity, combined with late maturity, means that population recovery from depletion is an extremely slow process.

Longevity is a defining feature of the sandbar shark's life history, with individuals capable of surviving for many decades. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is estimated at 34 years [am = 34 years] when individuals are maintained at the typical thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with the late age at puberty, means that a female may only produce a limited number of litters over her entire reproductive career, likely fewer than ten. Such a life-history strategy places a premium on adult and juvenile survival, as even modest increases in mortality from fishing or habitat degradation can drive rapid population declines. The combination of a large ultimate size, slow growth, very late reproduction, and extreme longevity makes the sandbar shark one of the most K-selected species among the coastal sharks, exhibiting life-history traits that are analogous to those of large marine mammals.
